newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: SAfrica maize exports above 700,000 T-shippers.
newsitem.headline: SAfrica maize exports above 700,000 T-shippers.

text.p: South African shipping sources said on Monday that over 700,000 tonnes of this season's maize had left the country for abroad up until the end of July, the bulk of it white grain.
However, small amounts of yellow maize -- used for animal feed -- had been shipped to the Middle East and more was expected to arrive in harbour soon.
"The yellow is only starting to go out now," one source at the country's main Durban port said. "Of all the maize we have shipped about 75 percent was white and the other 25 yellow."
Shippers said around 650,000 tonnes had left from the east coast-based Durban and some 56,000 tonnes from the smaller harbour of East London, situated further south on the coast.

An East London source said that two shiploads of white maize had already left the port, one having moved out over the weekend. He said no yellow maize had yet been shipped, nor were there any orders for it.
However, another 100,000 tonnes of white maize had been contracted for shipment out of East London in the period to early September.
One Durban shipper said that they were booked to export another 125,000 tonnes maize, comprising both white and yellow, in August.
The country's agricultural co-operatives said in May that they had been successful in selling 250,000 tonnes of yellow maize to Iran.

Near-dated yellow maize futures contracts continued down on the South African Futures Exchange (Safex) last week on expectations of a surplus. Of this year's total expected maize crop of 7.966 million tonnes, 3.633 million is expected to be yellow.
"Yellow prices are still under pressure. The market seems to be saying there is more yellow out there than it anticipated," said Rod Blondin, general manager of Safex's agricultural markets unit.
However, prices for white maize remained firm following rains early last week, concerns of some poor quality maize and continued worries of a shortage due to large-scale exports to drought-hit Kenya.

The National Maize Producers Organisation (Nampo) said last month that there would be a 476,000 tonne shortage of white maize this season. Some maize traders and millers have dismissed this as an attempt to inflate prices, while others have said there may be a small shortfall of around 100,000 tonnes.
Andre Ferreira, economist at Nampo, said that farmers had had to stop harvesting for a few days last week due to rains, which have already delayed the crop by some six weeks.
But he said over half the crop had by now been brought in.
"I would guess that about 60 percent of the crop has been harvested," Ferreira said.

Fears about the rapid and early build-up this year of the El Nino weather phenomenon, which in 1982/83 caused a severe drought in southern Africa, continued to feature in the market with millers saying they were signing forward contracts early.
But some traders said that even if El Nino did hit, its impact at the planting stage would be lessened by the high moisture content of the soil after two years of good rains.
Near-month white maize ended Friday at 635.00 from 626.00 the week before and December white rose during the week to 685.00 rand from 665.00.
September yellow closed Friday at 530.00 rand from 535.00 at the end of the previous week and December yellow was ended at 571.00 from 575.00.
